stem: A company wants to try foundation models from several providers, including Amazon, Anthropic, Meta and Mistral AI, through a single API, without provisioning or managing any infrastructure.
prompt: Which AWS service meets these requirements?

options.why: JumpStart offers many models, but it deploys them to endpoints on instances you choose and pay for, so there is infrastructure to manage.
Bedrock is fully managed and serverless, offering foundation models from Amazon and leading AI companies through one API.
AgentCore hosts and operates agents. It is not the service that provides API access to many providers' models.
Kendra is an intelligent enterprise search service; it does not provide access to foundation models.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to high-performing foundation models from Amazon (such as Amazon Nova and Titan) and third-party providers through a single API. It also offers capabilities to customize models, build RAG with knowledge bases, create agents, apply guardrails and evaluate models.
explanation.concept: Because Bedrock is serverless, there is no infrastructure to manage, and you can switch between models with minimal code changes.
explanation.examTip: Many FMs, one API, no infrastructure = Amazon Bedrock.

stem: A healthcare company's security team is concerned that prompts and responses sent to foundation models on Amazon Bedrock might be used to train those models or shared with model providers.
prompt: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock addresses this concern?

options.text: Bedrock publishes prompts publicly unless encryption is disabled.
options.why: Bedrock does not publish customer data. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest.

options.text: Bedrock only works if the company uploads its data to the model provider's own servers.
options.why: Model providers do not receive customer data through Bedrock. Models are run within AWS infrastructure.

options.text: Bedrock doesn't use prompts to train base models or share them with providers
options.why: AWS states that Bedrock does not store or use your prompts and completions to train AWS or third-party models, and does not distribute them to providers.

options.text: Bedrock shares all prompts with model providers to improve their models.
options.why: This is incorrect. Bedrock does not share customer prompts and responses with model providers for training.

explanation.answer: With Amazon Bedrock, your content is not used to improve the base models and is not shared with model providers. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and when you customize a model, Bedrock creates a private copy that only you can access.
explanation.concept: Additional controls include AWS PrivateLink for private connectivity, AWS KMS customer managed keys, IAM policies, and CloudTrail logging.
explanation.examTip: Bedrock: your prompts are not used to train base models or shared with providers.

stem: An ML team wants to build a generative AI solution where it controls the training code, the exact instance types for training and hosting, and the model weights, and it has the skills to manage this.
prompt: Which AWS service gives the MOST control for this team?

options.why: Bedrock fine-tuning is managed and simple, but it does not let you supply training code or choose instance types.
Canvas is a no-code tool for analysts; it hides training code and infrastructure choices.
Custom Model Import brings already-trained weights into Bedrock; it does not run custom training or let you pick hosting instances.
SageMaker AI gives full control over training scripts, instance types, model artifacts and inference containers.

explanation.answer: Amazon SageMaker AI is the choice when teams need deep control over the ML lifecycle: custom training code, distributed training, instance selection, model weights and custom inference containers. Amazon Bedrock is the choice for fully managed access to FMs with less operational work.
explanation.concept: Trade-off: Bedrock offers simplicity and speed; SageMaker AI offers flexibility and control at the cost of more operational responsibility.
explanation.examTip: Maximum control over training and hosting = SageMaker AI. Fully managed FM access = Bedrock.

stem: A data scientist wants to browse hundreds of pre-trained foundation models, compare them, deploy one to a SageMaker AI endpoint in a few clicks and fine-tune it, all inside SageMaker Studio.
prompt: Which capability should the data scientist use?

options.why: JumpStart is SageMaker AI's model hub, with pre-trained FMs that deploy to SageMaker endpoints and can be fine-tuned from Studio.
Canvas offers no-code ML and ready-made models, but it is not the Studio model hub for deploying and fine-tuning FMs on endpoints.
Playgrounds let you try Bedrock models in the console; they do not deploy models to SageMaker endpoints.
Model Registry catalogs your own trained model versions; it is not a hub of pre-trained foundation models.

explanation.answer: SageMaker JumpStart provides a catalog of pre-trained models, including popular open and proprietary foundation models, with one-click deployment to SageMaker AI endpoints and options to fine-tune and evaluate them in your account.
explanation.concept: Models deployed through JumpStart run on endpoints in your account, giving you control over instance types and network isolation, and you pay for the underlying instances.
explanation.examTip: Model hub inside SageMaker with one-click deploy and fine-tune = JumpStart.

stem: A team has built an AI agent using an open-source framework. It now needs to run the agent in production on AWS with secure session isolation, automatic scaling and support for long-running tasks, without managing servers.
prompt: Which AWS capability is designed for this?

options.why: Lambda is serverless, but functions have a short maximum duration and no built-in per-session isolation for long-running agents.
AgentCore Runtime is a secure, serverless environment for agents built with any framework, with session isolation and long-running support.
Bedrock Agents builds agents by configuration in Bedrock; it does not host an agent already written in an open-source framework.
Fargate could run the agent container, but the team would have to build session isolation, scaling and agent-specific operations itself.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a set of services for deploying and operating agents securely at scale with any framework and model. AgentCore Runtime hosts agents serverlessly with per-session isolation and support for extended execution, removing infrastructure management.
explanation.concept: Other AgentCore services: Memory, Gateway (turn APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools), Identity, Code Interpreter, Browser, Observability, Policy and Evaluations.
explanation.examTip: Run any-framework agents in production, serverless and isolated = AgentCore Runtime.

stem: A company has dozens of existing REST APIs and AWS Lambda functions. It wants agents to use them as tools through the Model Context Protocol without rewriting each one as an MCP server.
prompt: Which capability BEST meets this requirement?

options.why: Polly generates speech and has no role in tool integration.
Guardrails filter content and sensitive information. They do not convert APIs into tools.
AgentCore Gateway converts existing APIs and Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools that agents can discover and call.
Feature Store holds ML features and does not expose APIs as agent tools.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway lets you turn existing APIs, Lambda functions and services into MCP-compatible tools with minimal code, handling authentication and making tools discoverable to agents.
explanation.concept: Gateway pairs with AgentCore Identity for authentication and Policy in AgentCore for controlling which tools agents may call.
explanation.examTip: Existing APIs/Lambda → MCP tools for agents = AgentCore Gateway.

stem: A developer wants an open-source SDK for building AI agents in a few lines of code, where the developer provides a model, a prompt and a list of tools, and the model itself drives planning and tool use.
prompt: Which option matches this description?

options.why: Bedrock Agents is a managed, configuration-based service, not an open-source SDK you build with in code.
AgentCore provides services to run and operate agents; it is not the SDK used to write them.
Flows is a visual builder for predefined workflows, not a code-first agent SDK.
Strands Agents is an open-source SDK with a model-driven approach: you give it a model, a prompt and tools, and the model plans and calls tools.

explanation.answer: Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building agents with a model-driven approach. It supports models on Amazon Bedrock and other providers, tools including MCP servers, and multi-agent patterns, and agents built with it can be deployed to runtimes such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
explanation.concept: Framework choice (Strands, or other open-source frameworks) is separate from where agents run (for example AgentCore Runtime).
explanation.examTip: Open-source, model-driven agent SDK from AWS = Strands Agents.

stem: A product team compares building its own generative AI infrastructure with using AWS managed generative AI services.
prompt: Which advantage of AWS managed generative AI services is MOST accurate?

options.text: Lower barrier to entry and faster launch, with no infrastructure
options.why: Managed services provide models through APIs, so teams focus on the application instead of building infrastructure.

options.text: AWS becomes responsible for the content the application generates
options.why: Customers remain responsible for how they use models and for their application's outputs.

options.text: Models are automatically fine-tuned on each customer's data
options.why: Customization is optional and customer-driven; base models are not trained on customer data.

options.text: Usage costs stay fixed, regardless of how much is used
options.why: On-demand pricing is usage-based; costs grow with tokens processed.

explanation.answer: AWS generative AI services offer accessibility, a lower barrier to entry, efficiency, cost-effectiveness (pay as you go), speed to market and alignment with business objectives, because AWS manages models and infrastructure.
explanation.concept: Responsibility is shared: AWS secures the infrastructure and service, while customers are responsible for their data, access controls, prompts, guardrails and how outputs are used.
explanation.examTip: Managed GenAI services = faster, easier, no infrastructure. You still own responsible use.

stem: A company is matching AWS generative AI offerings to the people who will use them.
prompt: Which pairings are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Developers who need speech synthesis → Amazon Rekognition
options.why: Rekognition analyzes images and video. Speech synthesis is Amazon Polly.

options.text: Business analysts who want natural-language insights, dashboards and workflow automation → Amazon Quick
options.why: Amazon Quick is designed as an AI workspace for business users.

options.text: Business analysts who want natural-language insights → AWS CloudTrail
options.why: CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing and is not an insights tool.

options.text: Data scientists training custom models → AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports. Data scientists train models with SageMaker AI.

options.text: Developers building generative AI applications on managed foundation models → Amazon Bedrock
options.why: Bedrock provides FMs and building blocks such as knowledge bases, agents and guardrails for application developers.

explanation.answer: AWS offers generative AI tools for different personas: Amazon Quick for business users, Amazon Bedrock for developers building applications, SageMaker AI for data scientists and ML engineers, and Kiro and Amazon Q Developer for software developers.
explanation.concept: Matching the tool to the persona is a common exam pattern.
explanation.examTip: Business users → Quick. App developers → Bedrock. ML builders → SageMaker AI. Coders → Kiro / Q Developer.

stem: An agent must access a user's calendar in a third-party SaaS product and the company's internal APIs on that user's behalf. The security team wants agents to have managed identities and to use securely stored OAuth tokens rather than hard-coded credentials.
prompt: Which AWS capability is designed for this?

options.why: Polly generates speech and has no identity features.
AgentCore Identity manages agent identities and access, including securely obtaining and storing credentials such as OAuth tokens to act on behalf of users.
Knowledge Bases provide RAG over documents. They do not manage agent credentials.
Canvas is a no-code ML tool and does not handle agent authentication.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provides identity and access management for agents. It integrates with existing identity providers, manages agent identities, and securely handles credentials such as OAuth tokens and API keys so agents can access AWS and third-party services on behalf of users.
explanation.concept: Avoid embedding secrets in agent code or prompts. Combine managed identity with least-privilege permissions and policies controlling tool access.
explanation.examTip: Agent needs credentials or OAuth to act for users = AgentCore Identity.

stem: A software team wants AI assistance for writing, explaining, testing and upgrading code, integrated into IDEs and the command line, with awareness of AWS services.
prompt: Which AWS offerings are designed for this audience?

options.why: These are for building AI applications and hosting models, not AI coding assistance inside the IDE.

options.text: Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock Flows
options.why: Quick serves business users and Flows builds generative AI workflows; neither is an IDE coding assistant.
Q Developer assists with code in IDEs, the CLI and the console, and Kiro is AWS's agentic development environment.
These build and run AI agents for applications; they are not developer coding assistants.

explanation.answer: Generative AI for software development on AWS includes Amazon Q Developer (coding assistance, code transformation, security scans, AWS guidance) and Kiro (an agentic IDE with spec-driven development).
explanation.concept: These tools increase developer productivity, but generated code still needs review and testing.
explanation.examTip: Help writing and maintaining code = Amazon Q Developer / Kiro.

stem: A regulated financial firm is choosing where to build its generative AI applications. Its main concerns are security, compliance certifications and keeping data under its control.
prompt: Which benefit of AWS infrastructure for generative AI is MOST relevant?

options.text: AWS makes applications compliant automatically, with no customer duties
options.why: Under shared responsibility, customers must still configure and use services compliantly.

options.text: AWS runs every model on hardware dedicated to each customer
options.why: Managed services use AWS-operated infrastructure; data isolation comes from service controls, not dedicated hardware per customer.

options.text: Model providers get access to data so they can improve security
options.why: Bedrock does not share customer prompts or data with model providers.

options.text: Encryption, private networking, IAM and compliance programs
options.why: Security controls plus compliance certifications help regulated firms meet obligations while keeping control of their data, under shared responsibility.

explanation.answer: Benefits of AWS infrastructure for generative AI include security (encryption, IAM, VPC and AWS PrivateLink), compliance (many certifications and attestations available through AWS Artifact), responsible AI tools (Bedrock Guardrails, evaluation) and global, resilient infrastructure.
explanation.concept: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud; customers are responsible for security in the cloud, including data, access, configuration and application behavior.
explanation.examTip: AWS GenAI infrastructure benefits = security, compliance, responsibility tools, safety.

stem: A product manager with no coding skills wants to quickly compare how different foundation models respond to the same prompts and adjust settings such as temperature before engineers build anything.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock feature supports this?

options.text: The Amazon Bedrock playgrounds in the console
options.why: Playgrounds let anyone try models interactively, compare responses and adjust inference settings without code.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation jobs on a test set
options.why: Evaluation jobs need prepared datasets and configuration; they are for systematic comparison, not quick hands-on trials.
Batch inference runs large prompt sets asynchronously from S3; it is not an interactive way to try models.
Logging records requests for auditing; it provides no interface for trying models.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock provides console playgrounds (for chat, text and images) where users can experiment with models, compare responses side by side and tune inference parameters before writing code.
explanation.concept: Experimentation is an early step in the generative AI lifecycle. Promising prompts can then be saved in Prompt Management and evaluated systematically.
explanation.examTip: Try and compare models without code = Bedrock playgrounds.

stem: An analytics agent must run Python code to analyze uploaded CSV files, and a research agent must navigate websites and fill in web forms. The security team wants these capabilities isolated from other systems.
prompt: Which AgentCore capabilities address these needs?

options.why: These store conversation context and manage agent credentials; neither runs code or operates a browser.

options.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter and AgentCore Browser
options.why: Code Interpreter runs agent-generated code in a secure sandbox, and Browser gives agents an isolated, managed browser for websites.

options.text: AgentCore Gateway and Policy in AgentCore
options.why: These expose tools and control which tools agents may call; they do not execute code or browse websites.
These host the agent and trace its behavior; they do not provide the sandboxed code and browser tools.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore includes built-in tools: Code Interpreter, which lets agents securely execute code in isolated sandboxes, and Browser, a secure cloud browser runtime that lets agents navigate and interact with websites.
explanation.concept: Running agent-generated code or browsing untrusted websites carries risk, so isolation, least privilege and monitoring are essential.
explanation.examTip: Agent runs code → Code Interpreter. Agent uses websites → Browser.

stem: A team wants to create an agent quickly by configuring instructions, a foundation model, action groups that call AWS Lambda functions, and knowledge bases in the console, letting AWS manage the orchestration logic.
prompt: Which capability fits BEST?

options.why: Ground Truth is for data labeling, not building agents.
Comprehend analyzes text and cannot orchestrate agent actions.
Bedrock Agents provides a fully managed way to configure agents with instructions, action groups and knowledge bases, with AWS handling orchestration.
Trusted Advisor recommends account improvements and does not build agents.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Agents is a managed capability for building agents through configuration: you choose a model, write instructions, define action groups (backed by Lambda or API schemas) and attach knowledge bases. AWS manages prompt orchestration, tool calls and session state.
explanation.concept: Choose Bedrock Agents for fast, configuration-based agents; choose frameworks such as Strands Agents with AgentCore when you need code-level control and framework flexibility.
explanation.examTip: Configure-not-code agent with action groups and knowledge bases = Bedrock Agents.

references.title: Automate tasks with Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: A company wants to use an open-weight model that is not offered as a serverless model in Amazon Bedrock. It still wants to call the model through Bedrock's unified APIs alongside other Bedrock models.
prompt: Which approach supports this?

options.text: Deploy it on a SageMaker AI endpoint and call that endpoint
options.why: This works, but calls go through the SageMaker endpoint API, not Bedrock's unified APIs as required.

options.text: Fine-tune a similar Bedrock model to imitate it
options.why: Fine-tuning a different model does not give access to the open-weight model the company wants.

options.text: Ask AWS to add the model to the serverless catalog
options.why: The company cannot control what AWS adds; Bedrock already provides ways to bring in other models.

options.text: Use Bedrock Custom Model Import or Bedrock Marketplace
options.why: These bring additional supported models into Bedrock so they can be invoked through the same APIs.

explanation.answer: Beyond its serverless model catalog, Amazon Bedrock lets you use additional models: Custom Model Import brings in supported open-weight models you have customized elsewhere, and Bedrock Marketplace provides access to many more models deployed on managed endpoints, all usable through Bedrock APIs.
explanation.concept: Alternatively, SageMaker JumpStart or custom SageMaker AI endpoints host models outside Bedrock with full infrastructure control.
explanation.examTip: Use an extra or custom open-weight model via Bedrock APIs = Custom Model Import / Bedrock Marketplace.

stem: A team wants to use foundation models built by Amazon on Amazon Bedrock for text understanding and generation, image and video understanding, and image generation.
prompt: Which family of Amazon-built models should the team look at?

options.why: Amazon Nova is Amazon's family of foundation models on Bedrock, covering text, image and video understanding plus image and video generation.
AgentCore is a set of services for running agents, not a family of models.
Rekognition analyzes images and video with pre-trained APIs, but it does not generate text or images.
Q Developer is an AI coding assistant, not a family of foundation models.

explanation.answer: Amazon Nova is a family of foundation models from Amazon available in Amazon Bedrock. It includes understanding models of different sizes and costs for text and multimodal input, and creative models for image and video generation.
explanation.concept: Amazon Titan models (for example Titan Text Embeddings) are also available in Bedrock, alongside models from third-party providers.
explanation.examTip: Amazon's own FMs on Bedrock = Amazon Nova (and Titan for embeddings).

stem: A company runs many agents that call tools through AgentCore Gateway. Security wants centrally defined, enforceable rules, such as "refund tools may be called only for amounts under $500", applied outside the agents' own code.
prompt: Which capability is designed for this?

options.why: Knowledge Bases provide retrieval over documents and do not enforce tool-use rules.
Policy in AgentCore lets teams define rules that govern which tools agents can use and under what conditions, enforced at the gateway rather than in agent code.
Data Wrangler prepares training data and has no role in governing agent actions.
Polly converts text to speech. It has no capability to define or enforce rules on agent tool calls.

explanation.answer: Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides centralized, deterministic controls over agent actions: policies define which tools agents may call and with what parameters, and they are enforced when tool calls pass through AgentCore Gateway, independent of the model's reasoning.
explanation.concept: Deterministic policy enforcement complements probabilistic safeguards such as prompts and guardrails, which matters for agents that take real actions.
explanation.examTip: Enforce rules on agent tool calls outside the agent's code = Policy in AgentCore.

stem: A sales operations team wants AI agents that can research accounts across company data and the web, answer questions about pipeline dashboards, and automate repetitive tasks such as updating records, all from one workspace connected to the company's applications.
prompt: Which AWS offering is designed for this?

options.why: Q Developer helps software developers write and maintain code, not sales teams research accounts and dashboards.
Bedrock Agents is for developers building agents into applications; the sales team wants a ready-to-use workspace.
Amazon Quick brings AI agents, research, business intelligence and automation into one workspace for business teams.
Canvas lets analysts build ML models without code; it is not an agentic workspace for research and automation.

explanation.answer: Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace for business users. It combines chat agents, deep research, business intelligence with dashboards (Quick Sight), and automation of tasks and workflows, connected to company data and applications.
explanation.concept: Business users get generative AI benefits without building applications, while administrators control data access and permissions.
explanation.examTip: Business team + research + dashboards + automation in one place = Amazon Quick.

stem: A developer is reviewing what Amazon Bedrock provides beyond access to foundation models.
prompt: Which capabilities are part of Amazon Bedrock? (Select THREE.)

options.why: OS patching is handled by AWS Systems Manager, not Bedrock.

options.text: Guardrails to filter harmful content and sensitive information
options.why: Bedrock Guardrails applies configurable safeguards to prompts and responses.

options.text: Model customization such as fine-tuning and distillation
options.why: Bedrock supports customizing models with your data, including fine-tuning and distillation for supported models.

options.text: Knowledge Bases for retrieval augmented generation
options.why: Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages ingestion, embeddings, vector storage and retrieval for RAG.

options.text: Issuing public TLS certificates for websites
options.why: Certificates are issued by AWS Certificate Manager, not Bedrock.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock includes building blocks for generative AI applications: access to many FMs, Knowledge Bases (RAG), Agents and Flows, Guardrails, model customization (fine-tuning, continued pre-training, distillation), Model Evaluation, Prompt Management and batch inference.
explanation.concept: Using managed building blocks speeds development compared with assembling each piece yourself.
explanation.examTip: Bedrock = models + knowledge bases + agents + guardrails + customization + evaluation.

stem: A school district wants to deploy a generative AI tutor for students and needs to block inappropriate content, prevent discussion of certain topics, and filter out personal information.
prompt: Which AWS capability helps meet these safety requirements?

options.why: Comprehend can find PII in text, but it does not block inappropriate content or denied topics in model conversations.
Rekognition moderates images and video, not a text tutor's conversations.
Evaluation measures a model's behavior on test data; it does not block content in live conversations.
Guardrails provide content filters, denied topics and PII filters applied to both inputs and outputs.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails implements safeguards for generative AI applications: content filters for harmful categories, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information (PII) filters with blocking or masking, contextual grounding checks and automated reasoning checks. It can be applied across models.
explanation.concept: Safety is one of the benefits AWS infrastructure provides for generative AI, alongside security, compliance and responsible AI tooling.
explanation.examTip: Block harmful content, denied topics or PII = Bedrock Guardrails.

references.title: Detect and filter harmful content with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

stem: Two teams discuss hosting. Team A wants to call models without thinking about instances. Team B wants to choose GPU instance types, keep the model inside a specific VPC configuration it controls, and pay for the instances it runs.
prompt: Which services BEST fit each team?

options.text: A: Bedrock serverless models. B: SageMaker AI or JumpStart endpoints
options.why: Bedrock removes instance management, while SageMaker endpoints give Team B instance choice and networking control, billed per instance.

options.text: A: SageMaker AI endpoints. B: Bedrock serverless models
options.why: This is reversed: SageMaker endpoints require choosing instances, and Bedrock serverless models do not offer that.

options.text: A: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput. B: Bedrock serverless models
options.why: Neither Bedrock option lets Team B choose GPU instance types.

options.text: Both: Bedrock serverless models over AWS PrivateLink
options.why: PrivateLink keeps traffic private, but Team B still could not choose instance types or pay per instance.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock offers serverless model access billed per use, with no instance management. SageMaker JumpStart and SageMaker AI endpoints deploy models onto instances you choose and pay for, giving more control over hardware, networking and runtime.
explanation.concept: Cost profiles differ: serverless per-token pricing suits variable traffic, while dedicated instances can suit steady high-volume workloads or specialized requirements.
explanation.examTip: No instances = Bedrock. Choose instances and control networking = SageMaker AI / JumpStart.

stem: A company runs a production agent and wants to continuously measure qualities such as whether the agent completes tasks correctly, uses the right tools and stays helpful, based on real interactions.
prompt: Which approach BEST supports this?

options.text: A benchmark evaluation before launch, repeated once a year
options.why: Agent behavior changes as data, tools and usage change; yearly benchmark checks miss problems in real interactions.

options.text: Continuous evaluation of real interaction traces with AgentCore
options.why: Evaluating live traces on task completion, tool use and helpfulness shows how the agent actually performs over time.

options.text: CloudWatch metrics on request counts and errors
options.why: Operational metrics show load and failures, not whether tasks were completed correctly.

options.text: User thumbs-up ratings as the only signal of answer quality
options.why: User ratings are useful but sparse and do not show whether the right tools were used.

explanation.answer: Agents should be evaluated continuously on quality dimensions such as task completion, correctness, tool selection and helpfulness. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides observability (traces and metrics) and evaluation capabilities that score agent behavior on real interactions.
explanation.concept: Business-aligned agent metrics include task completion rate, cost per interaction and user satisfaction.
explanation.examTip: Measure agent quality on real interactions continuously = AgentCore Observability + Evaluations.

stem: A company that trains and self-hosts large models on AWS wants to reduce the cost of training and of high-volume inference using purpose-built AWS hardware.
prompt: Which AWS chips are designed for these workloads?

options.text: AWS Nitro Enclaves for training and AWS Snowball for inference
options.why: Nitro Enclaves isolate sensitive processing, and Snowball moves data physically. Neither is an ML accelerator.
Lambda is serverless compute for short functions and is not designed to train large models.

options.text: AWS Trainium for training and AWS Inferentia for inference
options.why: Trainium is designed for cost-efficient model training, and Inferentia is designed for high-performance, low-cost inference.

options.text: Amazon S3 Glacier for training and Amazon EBS for inference
options.why: These are storage services, not compute accelerators.

explanation.answer: AWS designs its own ML chips: AWS Trainium (for training) and AWS Inferentia (for inference), available through EC2 instance families such as Trn and Inf. They aim to provide better price performance than general-purpose GPUs for supported models.
explanation.concept: Purpose-built infrastructure is one way AWS reduces the cost of generative AI, alongside serverless pricing and capacity options in Bedrock.
explanation.examTip: Trainium = train. Inferentia = infer.

stem: An enterprise has agents written with several different open-source frameworks and using models from more than one provider. It wants a single set of AWS services to deploy and operate all of them securely.
prompt: Why is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore a good fit?

options.text: Agents are configured in the console instead of being coded
options.why: That describes Bedrock Agents. AgentCore runs agents written in code with any framework.

options.text: It requires every agent to use models hosted in Amazon Bedrock
options.why: AgentCore works with models inside or outside Bedrock.

options.text: It converts every agent to a single AWS framework
options.why: AgentCore runs existing agents without rewriting them in one framework.

options.text: Any framework or model works, with runtime, memory and identity
options.why: AgentCore is framework- and model-agnostic and adds runtime, memory, identity, gateway and observability services.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a set of composable services for running agents in production: Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, Code Interpreter, Browser, Observability, Policy and Evaluations. It works with popular open-source frameworks and with models inside or outside Amazon Bedrock.
explanation.concept: Separating the agent's logic (framework) from operational concerns (runtime, identity, observability) simplifies scaling many agents securely.
explanation.examTip: Operate any framework's agents securely at scale = Bedrock AgentCore.
